title: Biology
summary: Cell and genetics, human body systems, vitamins and minerals, diseases with pathogens, vectors and vaccines, plant physiology and classification, and branches of biology with ecology. Biology is the most-asked science area in CGL GA — mostly direct one-line facts.

subtopics.title: Cell, organelles and genetics
subtopics.concept:
### Discoveries about the cell
| Discovery | Scientist |
|---|---|
| Cell (in cork, 1665) | **Robert Hooke** |
| First living cells, bacteria (single-lens microscope) | **Antonie van Leeuwenhoek** |
| **Nucleus** (1831) | **Robert Brown** |
| **Cell theory** | **Schleiden** (plants) and **Schwann** (animals) |
| 'Omnis cellula e cellula' — new cells come from existing cells | **Rudolf Virchow** |

### Cell organelles
| Organelle | Function / nickname |
|---|---|
| **Mitochondria** | **Powerhouse of the cell** — aerobic respiration, ATP; have their own DNA |
| **Ribosomes** | **Protein synthesis** (no membrane) |
| **Lysosomes** | **'Suicide bags'** — digestive enzymes |
| **Golgi apparatus** | Packaging and secretion |
| **Endoplasmic reticulum** | Transport; rough ER (with ribosomes) makes proteins, smooth ER makes lipids |
| **Chloroplast** | **Photosynthesis** (plants only); has its own DNA |
| **Nucleus** | Control centre; holds chromosomes (DNA) |
| **Vacuole** | Storage; large in plant cells |
| **Cell wall** | Plants (**cellulose**), fungi (**chitin**) — absent in animal cells |

- **Prokaryotes** (bacteria, blue-green algae) have **no nuclear membrane** and no membrane-bound organelles. **Eukaryotes** have a true nucleus.
- Largest cell: **ostrich egg**. Longest cell: **nerve cell (neuron)**. Smallest cell: **Mycoplasma (PPLO)**. Mature mammalian **RBCs have no nucleus**.
- **Mitosis** — body growth and repair, gives **2 identical** cells. **Meiosis** — forms **gametes**, halves the chromosome number (4 cells).

### Genetics
- **Gregor Mendel** — **father of genetics**; experiments on **garden pea** (Pisum sativum); laws of dominance, segregation and independent assortment.
- **DNA double helix** — **Watson and Crick (1953)**, using X-ray data of Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins. DNA bases: A, T, G, C (RNA has **uracil** instead of thymine).
- Humans have **46 chromosomes (23 pairs)** in body cells: 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes. Gametes have 23.
- **Sex of the child is decided by the father**: XX = female, XY = male.
- **Haemophilia** and **colour blindness** are **X-linked** disorders — more common in males. **Down syndrome** — an extra chromosome 21 (trisomy 21).
- **Hugo de Vries** — mutation theory. **Darwin** — natural selection (*On the Origin of Species*, 1859). **Lamarck** — inheritance of acquired characters.
- **Har Gobind Khorana** — Nobel Prize 1968 for work on the genetic code.

tricks.title: Organelle nicknames: 'Power-Mito, Suicide-Lyso, Protein-Ribo, Packing-Golgi'
tricks.body: These four nicknames answer most organelle questions.

example.q: Which organelle is called the 'suicide bag' of the cell?
example.solution: Lysosome.

tricks.title: Cell discoverers in order
tricks.body: **Hooke** saw it (1665, dead cork) → **Leeuwenhoek** saw it alive → **Brown** saw the nucleus → **Schleiden–Schwann** made the theory → **Virchow** said cells come from cells.

mistakes: Saying Leeuwenhoek discovered the cell — Hooke coined the term; Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells.
Saying the mother decides the child's sex — the father's X or Y sperm does.
Giving animal cells a cell wall — only plants, fungi and bacteria have one.
subtopics.notes:
### The cell — discovery and the cell theory
**Robert Hooke** saw cork cells under his microscope in **1665** (book: *Micrographia*) — he named 'cells' but saw only dead walls. **Leeuwenhoek** first saw **living cells** ('animalcules'). **Robert Brown** discovered the **nucleus (1831)**. The **cell theory**: **Schleiden** (1838, plants) and **Schwann** (1839, animals) said all living things are made of cells; **Virchow (1855)** completed it — every cell arises from a pre-existing cell (*Omnis cellula e cellula*).

### Organelles — who does what
| Organelle | Job / title |
|---|---|
| **Mitochondria** | Respiration, ATP — **'powerhouse of the cell'**; has its own DNA |
| **Ribosome** | **Protein synthesis** — 'protein factory' |
| **Golgi body** | Packs and dispatches secretions — 'post office' |
| **Lysosome** | Digestive enzymes — **'suicide bags'** |
| **Chloroplast** | Photosynthesis (plastid); other plastids store colour/starch |
| **Nucleus** | Controls the cell; stores DNA — the 'brain' |
| **Vacuole** | Storage; big and central in plant cells |
| **Cell wall** | Rigid cellulose coat — **plant cells only** |
Plant vs animal cell: plant has a **cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole**; animal cells have **centrosomes** instead.

### Cell types and cell division
**Prokaryotes** (bacteria, blue-green algae) — no true nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles. **Eukaryotes** (plants, animals, fungi, protists) — true nucleus. Cell division: **mitosis** keeps the chromosome number (body growth, 46 → 46); **meiosis** halves it (gamete formation, 46 → 23) — the basis of sexual reproduction.

### Genetics — the science of heredity
**Gregor Mendel**, the **father of genetics**, worked on garden pea (*Pisum sativum*) and gave the laws of inheritance — dominant vs recessive traits. **Watson and Crick (1953)** gave the **DNA double-helix model**; a **gene** is a stretch of DNA coding a trait. Humans carry **46 chromosomes = 23 pairs**; the **23rd pair decides sex — XX female, XY male**, so the **father determines the child's sex**. Blood groups too are inherited traits.

### Cell records and blood cells
- **Largest human cell** — the **ovum** (egg); **longest** — the **nerve cell** (up to a metre).
- **RBC** (red blood cells): biconcave, **no nucleus**, carry oxygen on **haemoglobin** (iron); live about **120 days**.
- **WBC**: the defence cells (immunity); **platelets**: clot the blood.
- Normal counts: RBC ≈ 5 million per mm³, WBC ≈ 6,000–8,000 per mm³.

### Quick revision
- Hooke named cells (1665); Leeuwenhoek saw living ones; Brown found the nucleus; Schleiden + Schwann + Virchow = cell theory.
- Powerhouse–mitochondria; protein factory–ribosome; suicide bag–lysosome; post office–Golgi.
- Mitosis 46→46; meiosis 46→23; XX female, XY male; father decides sex.
- Mendel = father of genetics (pea plant); Watson & Crick = DNA double helix.
- Largest human cell–ovum; longest–nerve cell; RBC survives ~120 days.

patterns.name: Cell theory and discoverers
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who discovered the cell / nucleus / living cells', 'the cell theory was given by…', 'omnis cellula e cellula' attribution, year-based questions (1665, 1831, 1855).
patterns.logic:
1. Timeline: 1665 Hooke (cork, named cells) → Leeuwenhoek (living cells) → 1831 Robert Brown (nucleus) → 1838–39 Schleiden + Schwann (theory) → 1855 Virchow (cells from cells).
2. Trap: Hooke saw dead cork walls; the LIVING cells credit goes to Leeuwenhoek.
3. Latin tag *omnis cellula e cellula* belongs to Virchow.
Why: each scientist has exactly one signature fact — match the year and the noun.

example.q: The **cell theory** was proposed by —
example.solution: **Schleiden and Schwann** (1838–39), completed by Virchow. Hooke only named the cell.

patterns.name: Organelle ↔ function/nickname
patterns.howToSpot: 'Powerhouse of the cell', 'suicide bags', 'which organelle makes protein / packages secretions', 'which organelle has its own DNA'.
patterns.logic:
1. Nickname table: powerhouse–mitochondria; protein factory–ribosome; post office–Golgi; suicide bag–lysosome; kitchen–chloroplast; brain–nucleus.
2. Special facts: mitochondria and chloroplasts have their OWN DNA; RBCs are the odd cells WITHOUT a nucleus.
3. Photosynthesis needs chloroplast + chlorophyll; respiration is the mitochondrion's job.
Why: the question is always one nickname or one job — recall the pair, don't reason.

example.q: Which organelle is called the **'suicide bag'** of the cell?
example.solution: **Lysosome** — its enzymes digest the cell itself if the membrane bursts, hence the nickname.

patterns.name: Prokaryote vs eukaryote, plant vs animal cell
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is a prokaryote', 'bacteria lack a true nucleus', 'cell wall is made of cellulose in…', 'which structure is absent in animal cells'.
patterns.logic:
1. Prokaryote = no true nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles (bacteria, blue-green algae); eukaryote = everything else.
2. Plant-only structures: cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts, large central vacuole. Animal-only: centrosome.
3. 'Absent in animal cells' almost always answers cell wall or chloroplast.

example.q: The **cell wall** of a plant cell is made of —
example.solution: **Cellulose** — absent in animal cells. Chitin instead builds the fungal wall.

patterns.name: Cell division and chromosome numbers
patterns.howToSpot: 'The human body cell has how many chromosomes', 'chromosome number in a gamete', 'mitosis vs meiosis', 'which division keeps the number the same'.
patterns.logic:
1. Human body cell = 46 chromosomes (23 pairs); gamete = 23 — meiosis halves it.
2. Mitosis: growth and repair, number preserved (46→46). Meiosis: gamete formation, number halved (46→23).
3. Sex chromosomes: 22 pairs are autosomes; the 23rd pair (XX/XY) decides sex — the father's sperm decides it.

example.q: A human **gamete** contains how many chromosomes?
example.solution: **23** — meiosis halves the body-cell number of 46; fertilisation restores 46.

patterns.name: Genetics: Mendel, DNA, inheritance
patterns.howToSpot: 'Father of genetics', 'the DNA double helix model was given by…', 'Mendel worked on which plant', 'who determines the sex of a child', 'a gene is a segment of…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Mendel = father of genetics; plant = garden pea (*Pisum sativum*); laws of dominance and segregation.
2. DNA double helix — Watson and Crick, 1953; gene = segment of DNA.
3. Sex determination: mother always gives X; father gives X (girl) or Y (boy) — so the FATHER decides.
Why: one name + one organism + one year is the whole question.

example.q: **Watson and Crick** are famous for —
example.solution: The **double-helix model of DNA** (1953). Mendel is the genetics-father; Crick later also worked on the genetic code.

patterns.name: Blood cells and cell records
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which blood cells lack a nucleus', 'lifespan of RBC', 'which cells fight infection', 'largest / longest cell in the human body', 'which cell carries oxygen'.
patterns.logic:
1. RBC: no nucleus, biconcave, haemoglobin + iron, oxygen transport, ~120-day life.
2. WBC: defence/immunity; platelets: clotting (the third, fragment-type cell).
3. Records: ovum = largest human cell; nerve cell = longest.

example.q: The average lifespan of a human **red blood cell** is about —
example.solution: **120 days**; worn-out RBCs are destroyed mainly in the spleen (the 'graveyard of RBCs').

subtopics.title: Human body — organs, blood, digestion, glands
subtopics.concept:
### Record-holders of the human body
| Fact | Answer |
|---|---|
| Largest organ | **Skin** |
| Largest gland / largest internal organ | **Liver** |
| Longest bone | **Femur** (thigh bone) |
| Smallest bone | **Stapes** (middle ear) |
| Bones in an adult | **206** (about 300 at birth; many fuse) |
| Strongest/hardest substance | **Tooth enamel** |
| Master gland | **Pituitary** |
| Largest part of the brain | **Cerebrum** |
| Functional unit of the kidney | **Nephron** |
| Structural and functional unit of the nervous system | **Neuron** |
| Normal body temperature | **37 °C (98.6 °F)** |
| Normal blood pressure | About **120/80 mm Hg** |
| Normal resting heart rate | About **72 beats per minute** |

### Blood and circulation
- **William Harvey** described the circulation of blood.
- **RBCs** carry oxygen with **haemoglobin (iron-containing)**, live about **120 days**, are made in **red bone marrow**; the **spleen** is the 'graveyard of RBCs'. **WBCs** fight infection (immunity). **Platelets** help **clotting**.
- Blood groups — **Karl Landsteiner** (ABO). **O** is the **universal donor** (O negative, strictly) and **AB** the **universal recipient** (AB positive, strictly). The **Rh factor** was also found by Landsteiner and Wiener (named after the rhesus monkey).
- The human **heart** has **4 chambers**; the **SA node** is the natural **pacemaker**. Arteries carry blood **away** from the heart (all oxygenated except the pulmonary artery); veins carry blood **to** the heart (all deoxygenated except the pulmonary vein).

### Digestion
| Where | Secretion / enzyme | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Mouth | **Salivary amylase (ptyalin)** | Starch → maltose |
| Stomach | **HCl + pepsin** | Kills germs; proteins → peptides |
| Liver | **Bile** (stored in the **gall bladder**) | **Emulsifies fats** — contains no enzyme |
| Pancreas | Trypsin, lipase, amylase | Proteins, fats, starch |
| Small intestine | Villi | Most **absorption** of digested food |
| Large intestine | — | Absorbs **water** |

- The **small intestine** is the longest part of the alimentary canal.

### Nervous and endocrine systems
- **Cerebrum** — intelligence, memory, voluntary actions. **Cerebellum** — **balance and coordination**. **Medulla oblongata** — involuntary actions (**heartbeat, breathing**, swallowing).

| Gland | Hormone | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Pituitary** | Growth hormone and others | 'Master gland' |
| **Thyroid** | **Thyroxine** (needs iodine) | Deficiency → goitre |
| **Pancreas** (islets of Langerhans) | **Insulin** (β-cells), glucagon (α-cells) | Insulin **lowers blood sugar**; lack → **diabetes mellitus** |
| **Adrenal** | **Adrenaline** | 'Fight or flight' hormone |
| **Testes / ovaries** | Testosterone / oestrogen, progesterone | Sex hormones |

- The **pancreas** is both an endocrine and an exocrine gland. Insulin was isolated by **Banting and Best** (1921).
- In the **eye**, the **retina** holds the image; the **cornea** is what is donated in eye donation.
- The **lungs'** air sacs (**alveoli**) are the site of gas exchange.

tricks.title: Blood group giving: 'O gives, AB takes'
tricks.body: **O** has no A/B antigens → can **give** to all. **AB** has no anti-A/anti-B antibodies → can **take** from all.

example.q: The universal recipient blood group is?
example.solution: AB.

tricks.title: Brain parts: 'Cerebrum thinks, Cerebellum balances, Medulla keeps you alive'
tricks.body: Thinking/memory — cerebrum; balance/posture — cerebellum; heartbeat/breathing — medulla oblongata.

mistakes: Saying bile contains digestive enzymes — it only emulsifies fats.
Answering thyroid for the master gland — it is the pituitary.
Naming the heart or liver as the largest organ — skin is the largest organ; liver is the largest gland/internal organ.
subtopics.notes:
### Body records — the standard list
| Record | Answer |
|---|---|
| Largest organ | **Skin** |
| Largest gland / largest internal organ | **Liver** |
| Largest endocrine gland | **Thyroid** |
| Longest bone | **Femur** (thigh) |
| Smallest bone | **Stapes** (middle ear) |
| Smallest muscle | **Stapedius** (ear) |
| Strongest muscle (by force) | **Jaw (masseter)** |
| Bones in an adult | **206** |
| Bones in a newborn | about **300** (many fuse later) |
| Ribs | **12 pairs = 24** |
| Normal body temperature | **37 °C (98.6 °F)** |

### Blood and circulation
Blood ≈ 5 litres. **Plasma** (55%, the liquid), **RBC** (oxygen on haemoglobin), **WBC** (defence), **platelets** (clotting). **Blood groups**: ABO + Rh; **O− is the universal donor, AB+ the universal recipient**. The **heart** has 4 chambers (2 atria + 2 ventricles); its natural **pace-maker is the SA node**; humans have **double circulation** (blood passes through the heart twice per loop). Blood pressure is measured with a **sphygmomanometer**; normal ≈ **120/80 mm Hg**. A resting heart beats ≈ **72 times a minute**.

### Digestive system — organ by organ
Mouth: **salivary amylase** starts starch digestion. Stomach: **HCl** + **pepsin** (protein); a mucous lining saves the stomach from itself. Liver makes **bile** (stored in the gall bladder — **no enzymes**, it only **emulsifies fat**). Pancreas sends **trypsin** (protein) and **lipase** (fat). The **small intestine** is the real digestion + absorption site (villi); the large intestine absorbs only water.

### Endocrine glands — hormones
**Pituitary** = 'master gland' (growth hormone; under- or over-secretion gives dwarfism/gigantism). **Thyroid** = **thyroxine (contains iodine)** — deficiency causes **goitre**; **pancreas** = **insulin** (from the islets of Langerhans) controls blood sugar — its failure is **diabetes**; **adrenal** = adrenaline (the 'fight-or-flight' hormone); testes/ovaries = testosterone/estrogen.

### Excretion and the brain
**Kidneys** filter the blood in about a million **nephrons** each; urine (urea + water + salts) reaches the bladder. The **brain**: **cerebrum** (thinking, largest part), **cerebellum** (balance, posture), **medulla oblongata** (involuntary heartbeat/breathing — a spine injury there is fatal); reflex actions are handled by the **spinal cord** without waiting for the brain.

### Quick revision
- 206 adult bones; stapes smallest, femur longest; skin largest organ; liver largest gland.
- O− universal donor, AB+ universal recipient; SA node = pace-maker; BP 120/80 (sphygmomanometer).
- Bile has no enzymes (emulsifies fat); HCl + pepsin in stomach; villi absorb in the small intestine.
- Pituitary master gland; thyroxine needs iodine; insulin from pancreas fights diabetes; adrenaline = fight-or-flight.
- Cerebrum thinks, cerebellum balances, medulla keeps the heart beating.

patterns.name: Body records (largest/smallest/number)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Largest gland / largest organ / longest bone / smallest bone', 'how many bones does an adult have', 'which muscle is the smallest', number-of-ribs questions.
patterns.logic:
1. Records: skin = largest organ; liver = largest gland (and largest internal organ); thyroid = largest ENDOCRINE gland; femur = longest bone; stapes = smallest bone; stapedius = smallest muscle.
2. Numbers: adult 206 bones, newborn ≈ 300, ribs 12 pairs.
3. Trap: 'largest gland' = liver; 'largest endocrine gland' = thyroid; both are often mixed.
Why: pure recall — keep one list, test the three largest-X pairs against each other.

example.q: The **smallest bone** in the human body is —
example.solution: **Stapes** in the middle ear (about 3 mm). The smallest muscle, stapedius, sits right beside it.

patterns.name: Blood, groups and circulation
patterns.howToSpot: 'Universal donor / recipient', 'which blood cells fight infection / help clotting', 'pace-maker of the heart', 'how many chambers does the heart have', instrument for BP.
patterns.logic:
1. Cells: RBC carry oxygen; WBC defend; platelets clot.
2. Groups: O− universal donor; AB+ universal recipient; Rh factor decides +/−.
3. Heart: 4 chambers; SA node = pace-maker; double circulation in humans.
4. BP instrument = sphygmomanometer; normal 120/80 mm Hg; pulse ≈ 72/min resting.

example.q: Which blood group is the **universal recipient**?
example.solution: **AB+** — it carries no anti-A or anti-B antibodies. O− is the universal donor counterpart.

patterns.name: Organ ↔ secretion/function
patterns.howToSpot: 'Insulin is secreted by…', 'bile is produced in… / stored in…', 'which organ filters the blood', 'HCl is secreted in…', 'nephron belongs to…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Digestive secretions: mouth–salivary amylase; stomach–HCl + pepsin; liver–bile (stored in gall bladder, no enzymes); pancreas–trypsin + lipase (+ insulin from islets of Langerhans).
2. Kidney: filtration unit = nephron; brain parts: cerebrum–thinking, cerebellum–balance, medulla–involuntary control.
3. 'Bile stored where' = gall bladder; 'bile made where' = liver — split them.

example.q: **Bile**, which helps digest fats, is produced by the —
example.solution: **Liver** (largest gland) and stored in the gall bladder; it emulsifies fat but contains no enzymes.

patterns.name: Hormone ↔ gland and deficiency
patterns.howToSpot: 'Insulin / thyroxine / adrenaline is secreted by', 'master gland', 'which hormone controls blood sugar', 'deficiency of growth hormone causes…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Master gland–pituitary (growth hormone); thyroid–thyroxine (iodine; low → goitre); pancreas–insulin (diabetes); adrenal–adrenaline (fight-or-flight).
2. Sex hormones: testes–testosterone, ovaries–estrogen.
3. Link each hormone to its imbalance: dwarfism/gigantism–growth hormone, goitre–thyroxine, diabetes–insulin.
Why: gland–hormone–disease is a fixed triangle; any corner can be asked.

example.q: Which gland is called the **'master gland'**?
example.solution: **Pituitary** — its hormones steer the other endocrine glands, including the thyroid and adrenals.

patterns.name: Digestion steps and enzymes
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which enzyme digests protein / starch / fat', 'where is food fully digested and absorbed', 'function of villi', 'which juice has no enzyme', 'peristalsis is…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Enzyme-to-food: amylase–starch, pepsin/trypsin–protein, lipase–fat.
2. Small intestine = final digestion + absorption (villi increase area); large intestine = water only.
3. Bile = no enzymes, emulsifies fat; peristalsis = wave-like muscle movement pushing food.

example.q: Digested food is absorbed mainly in the —
example.solution: **Small intestine**, through millions of villi that multiply the absorbing surface. The large intestine takes up only water and salts.

patterns.name: Body numbers (computed)
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many times does the heart beat in a day', 'normal body temperature in °F', 'how much blood does an adult have', questions needing 72 × 60 or 37 → 98.6 conversion.
patterns.logic:
1. Heart: 72 beats/min → 72 × 60 × 24 = 103,680 beats/day.
2. Temperature: 37 °C = 98.6 °F (F = 9C/5 + 32).
3. Blood volume ≈ 5 litres; RBC count ≈ 5 million/mm³; WBC ≈ 6,000–8,000/mm³.
4. Compute the arithmetic in your head by splitting: 72 × 60 = 4,320; × 24 ≈ 1.04 lakh.

example.q: At a resting rate of **72 beats per minute**, the heart beats about how many times a **day**?
example.solution: 72 × 60 × 24 = **103,680** — roughly 1 lakh beats a day, pumping thousands of litres.

subtopics.title: Vitamins, minerals and nutrition
subtopics.concept:
### Vitamins
| Vitamin | Chemical name | Deficiency disease | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Retinol | **Night blindness**, xerophthalmia | Carrot, milk, fish-liver oil |
| **B1** | **Thiamine** | **Beriberi** | Whole grains |
| **B2** | Riboflavin | Cracked lips and mouth corners | Milk, eggs |
| **B3** | Niacin | **Pellagra** (the '3 D's' — dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia) | Groundnut, meat |
| **B9** | Folic acid | Anaemia | Green leafy vegetables |
| **B12** | **Cobalamin** (contains **cobalt**) | **Pernicious anaemia** | Animal foods |
| **C** | **Ascorbic acid** | **Scurvy** (bleeding gums) | **Amla**, citrus fruits |
| **D** | **Calciferol** | **Rickets** (children), osteomalacia (adults) | **Sunlight**, fish oil |
| **E** | **Tocopherol** | Reproductive problems/sterility; an **antioxidant** | Vegetable oils, nuts |
| **K** | Phylloquinone | **Blood does not clot** (haemorrhage) | Green leafy vegetables |

- **Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K**. **Water-soluble: B-complex and C** (not stored; C is destroyed by heating).
- Vitamin D is made in the **skin in sunlight**. The word 'vitamine' was coined by **Casimir Funk**.

### Minerals
| Mineral | Role / deficiency |
|---|---|
| **Iron** | Haemoglobin; deficiency → **anaemia** |
| **Iodine** | Thyroxine; deficiency → **goitre** |
| **Calcium, phosphorus** | Bones and teeth |
| **Sodium, potassium** | Nerve impulses, fluid balance |
| **Fluorine** | Tooth enamel (excess → fluorosis) |

### Macronutrients
- Energy per gram: **fat about 9 kcal**, carbohydrate about 4 kcal, protein about 4 kcal.
- **Proteins** are 'body-building' foods; **carbohydrates** are the main energy source; **roughage (fibre)** helps bowel movement.
- **Kwashiorkor** — protein deficiency (swollen belly); **marasmus** — deficiency of both protein and calories.

tricks.title: Fat-soluble vitamins: 'KADE' (or 'ADEK')
tricks.body: A, D, E, K dissolve in fat and are stored in the body; B and C dissolve in water.

tricks.title: Deficiency pairs: 'A-Andha (night blind), B1-Beriberi, C-sCurvy, D-Deformed bones (rickets), K-Klotting'
tricks.body: Add **B3 — Pellagra** ('3 D's) and **B12 — Pernicious anaemia** (cobalt).

example.q: Deficiency of which vitamin causes beriberi?
example.solution: Vitamin B1 (thiamine).

mistakes: Linking scurvy to vitamin D — scurvy is vitamin C; rickets is vitamin D.
Calling vitamin C fat-soluble — it is water-soluble and destroyed by cooking heat.
Mixing up kwashiorkor (protein only) and marasmus (protein + calories).
subtopics.notes:
### Vitamins → deficiency diseases (the top table)
| Vitamin | Chemical name | Deficiency disease | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Retinol | **Night blindness**, xerophthalmia | Carrot, papaya, milk |
| **B₁** | Thiamine | **Beriberi** | Whole grains, pulses |
| **B₂** | Riboflavin | Cheilosis (cracked lips) | Milk, eggs |
| **B₃** | Niacin | **Pellagra** (3 Ds) | Groundnut |
| **B₁₂** | Cyanocobalamin | **Pernicious anaemia** | Meat, milk |
| **C** | Ascorbic acid | **Scurvy** (bleeding gums) | Amla, citrus |
| **D** | Calciferol | **Rickets** (children), osteomalacia (adults) | Sunlight, fish oil |
| **E** | Tocopherol | Sterility | Wheat germ |
| **K** | Phylloquinone | **Poor clotting** | Green leafy vegetables |
**Fat-soluble**: **A, D, E, K** (stored in the body — excess can harm). **Water-soluble**: **B-complex and C** (washed out daily). **Casimir Funk (1912)** coined the word 'vitamine'. Sunlight on the skin makes **vitamin D**. Cooking destroys vitamin C most easily.

### Minerals → deficiency
**Iron** → **anaemia** (haemoglobin is iron-based); **iodine** → **goitre** (thyroxine); **calcium** → weak bones/teeth; **phosphorus** → bones + ATP; **fluorine** → too little causes dental caries, too much causes **fluorosis**; **sodium and potassium** → nerve and muscle function. Zinc: wound healing and immunity.

### Malnutrition — the two classics
**Kwashiorkor**: protein deficiency *with* adequate calories — swollen belly, oedema, thin limbs, in children 1–3 years. **Marasmus**: deficiency of *both* protein and calories — the child is all skin and bones, under one year old. One-line hold: **kwashiorkor = swollen, marasmus = shrunken**. Obesity is the opposite imbalance; **roughage** (fibre) prevents constipation.

### Food energy — the numbers
| Component | Energy |
|---|---|
| Carbohydrate | **4 kcal/g** |
| Protein | **4 kcal/g** |
| Fat | **9 kcal/g** |
Fat carries more than twice the energy per gram — hence a **30 g** fat snack gives 30 × 9 = 270 kcal. A balanced diet splits roughly 60% carbohydrates, 25–30% fat, 10–15% protein of the calories. **Basal metabolic rate (BMR)** is the resting burn; an adult needs ≈ 2,000–2,500 kcal/day.

### Quick revision
- A–night blindness, B₁–beriberi, B₃–pellagra, B₁₂–pernicious anaemia, C–scurvy, D–rickets, E–sterility, K–clotting.
- Fat-soluble A D E K; water-soluble B and C; 'vitamine' = Casimir Funk; vitamin D from sunlight.
- Iron–anaemia, iodine–goitre, calcium–bones, fluorine–caries/fluorosis.
- Kwashiorkor = protein (swollen); marasmus = protein + calories (shrunken).
- Energy: carb 4, protein 4, fat 9 kcal/g.

patterns.name: Vitamin → deficiency disease
patterns.howToSpot: 'Scurvy is caused by deficiency of…', 'rickets / beriberi / night blindness / pernicious anaemia', wrong-pair questions on the vitamin table.
patterns.logic:
1. Sing the ladder: A–night blindness, B₁–beriberi, B₃–pellagra, B₁₂–pernicious anaemia, C–scurvy, D–rickets, E–sterility, K–clotting.
2. Alphabet anchor: C = Citrus = scurvy (sailors); D = sun = rickets; K = Koagulation = clotting.
3. In wrong-pair questions, check D–rickets and C–scurvy first — they are the usual deliberate swaps.
Why: fixed pairs, zero logic — pure table recall.

example.q: **Pernicious anaemia** is caused by the deficiency of —
example.solution: **Vitamin B₁₂ (cyanocobalamin)**. Ordinary iron-deficiency anaemia is a different, more common condition.

patterns.name: Vitamin sources and fat/water solubility
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which vitamins are fat-soluble', 'which vitamin is made in the skin by sunlight', 'rich source of vitamin C', 'which vitamin is destroyed by cooking'.
patterns.logic:
1. Fat-soluble = **A, D, E, K** (they store in the liver/fat); water-soluble = B-complex, C.
2. Sunlight → vitamin D in the skin; cooking destroys **vitamin C** the most.
3. Sources: A–carrot/papaya, C–amla/citrus, D–fish oil/sun, K–green leafy vegetables.

example.q: Which set contains **only fat-soluble** vitamins?
example.solution: **A, D, E, K** — remember the word KEDA/ADKE. B-complex and C wash out with water every day.

patterns.name: Mineral → deficiency/role
patterns.howToSpot: 'Goitre is due to deficiency of…', 'anaemia is caused by lack of…', 'which mineral builds bones and teeth', 'fluorosis is due to excess…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Iron–anaemia (haemoglobin); iodine–goitre (thyroxine); calcium+phosphorus–bones/teeth; fluorine–caries (less) or fluorosis (more).
2. Sodium/potassium–nerve signals; zinc–healing and immunity.
3. Both 'too little' and 'too much' of fluorine harm — a favourite trick option.

example.q: **Anaemia** (low haemoglobin) most commonly results from the deficiency of —
example.solution: **Iron** — haemoglobin is an iron pigment, so iron-poor blood carries less oxygen (fatigue, pale skin).

patterns.name: Malnutrition: kwashiorkor vs marasmus
patterns.howToSpot: 'Kwashiorkor is caused by deficiency of…', 'swollen belly disease of children', 'difference between kwashiorkor and marasmus', protein-calorie malnutrition questions.
patterns.logic:
1. **Kwashiorkor**: protein deficient, calories adequate → oedema, swollen belly, thin limbs (age 1–3).
2. **Marasmus**: protein AND calories deficient → skin-and-bones, no swelling (below 1 year).
3. Memory line: kwashiorkor = swollen, marasmus = shrunken.

example.q: A child with a **swollen belly** but relatively adequate calorie intake suffers from —
example.solution: **Kwashiorkor** — protein deficiency; the swelling is oedema. Marasmus children are instead wasted and shrunken.

patterns.name: Food energy values (computed)
patterns.howToSpot: 'How much energy does 1 g of fat/carbohydrate give', a snack's total calories from given grams, 'which nutrient gives maximum energy', BMR questions.
patterns.logic:
1. Fixed values: carbohydrate 4 kcal/g, protein 4 kcal/g, **fat 9 kcal/g**.
2. Fat gives the most energy per gram — the standard 'maximum energy' answer.
3. Compute totals part-wise: (fat g × 9) + (carb g × 4) + (protein g × 4); split multiplication into tens to stay fast.

example.q: A snack has **20 g fat** and **10 g carbohydrate**. Its energy is about —
example.solution: 20 × 9 + 10 × 4 = 180 + 40 = **220 kcal** — fat dominates because it carries 9 kcal/g.

patterns.name: Vitamin history and misc facts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who coined the word vitamin', 'which vitamin is called ascorbic acid', chemical names of vitamins, 'deficiency of which vitamin affects gums'.
patterns.logic:
1. **Casimir Funk** coined 'vitamine' (1912).
2. Chemical names: A–retinol, B₁–thiamine, B₂–riboflavin, B₁₂–cyanocobalamin, C–ascorbic acid, D–calciferol, E–tocopherol, K–phylloquinone.
3. Bleeding gums = scurvy = vitamin C (ascorbic acid) — the acid name is the giveaway.

example.q: The word **'vitamine'** was coined by —
example.solution: **Casimir Funk (1912)**. He thought all such factors were amines; the final 'e' was later dropped.

subtopics.title: Diseases, pathogens, vectors and vaccines
subtopics.concept:
### Diseases by pathogen
| Pathogen | Diseases |
|---|---|
| **Bacteria** | **Tuberculosis**, **cholera**, **typhoid**, **diphtheria**, **tetanus**, **whooping cough** (pertussis), **leprosy**, **plague**, bacterial pneumonia |
| **Viruses** | **AIDS (HIV)**, **polio**, **measles**, mumps, **chickenpox**, **smallpox**, **rabies**, hepatitis, influenza, **dengue**, chikungunya, common cold, COVID-19 |
| **Protozoa** | **Malaria** (*Plasmodium*), **kala-azar** (*Leishmania*), amoebic dysentery (*Entamoeba*), sleeping sickness (*Trypanosoma*) |
| **Fungi** | **Ringworm**, athlete's foot |
| **Worms (helminths)** | **Filariasis / elephantiasis** (*Wuchereria*), ascariasis |

### Vectors
| Vector | Disease(s) |
|---|---|
| **Female Anopheles** mosquito | **Malaria** |
| **Aedes** mosquito (*A. aegypti*) | **Dengue**, **chikungunya**, yellow fever, Zika |
| **Culex** mosquito | **Filariasis**, Japanese encephalitis |
| **Rat flea** | **Plague** |
| **Sandfly** | **Kala-azar** |
| **Tsetse fly** | **Sleeping sickness** |
| Housefly | Carries germs of cholera, typhoid (mechanically) |

- **Rabies** (hydrophobia) spreads through the bite of an infected dog or other mammal.

### Vaccines, drugs and discoverers
| Discovery | Scientist |
|---|---|
| **Smallpox vaccine** (1796) — first vaccine | **Edward Jenner** |
| **Rabies vaccine**, pasteurisation, germ theory | **Louis Pasteur** |
| **TB bacterium** (1882), cholera bacterium | **Robert Koch** |
| **Penicillin** (1928) — first antibiotic | **Alexander Fleming** |
| Injectable (killed) **polio vaccine** | **Jonas Salk** |
| **Oral polio vaccine** | **Albert Sabin** |
| Malaria is spread by mosquitoes (Nobel 1902) | **Ronald Ross** |
| Blood groups | **Karl Landsteiner** |
| First human heart transplant (1967) | **Christiaan Barnard** |

- **BCG** — tuberculosis; **DPT** — diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus; **MMR** — measles, mumps, rubella.
- **Smallpox** was declared **eradicated** by WHO in **1980**. India was certified **polio-free** in **2014**.
- Diagnostic tests: **Widal — typhoid**, **ELISA — HIV/AIDS**, **Mantoux — tuberculosis**.
- **Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on viruses.**
- Non-communicable: diabetes, hypertension, cancer (**leukaemia** = blood cancer). **Jaundice** affects the **liver**; **conjunctivitis** — eyes; **glaucoma** / **cataract** — eyes; **arthritis** — joints.

tricks.title: Bacterial diseases: 'TB, Cholera, Typhoid, Diphtheria, Tetanus, Leprosy, Plague, Pertussis'
tricks.body: If the disease is in this list it is bacterial; the rest of the common ones (polio, measles, AIDS, dengue, rabies, chickenpox, hepatitis) are viral. Malaria and kala-azar are protozoan.

example.q: Which of these is a viral disease: typhoid, cholera, measles, tetanus?
example.solution: Measles.

tricks.title: Mosquito map: 'Anopheles-Malaria, Aedes-Dengue, Culex-Filaria'
tricks.body: **A**edes also spreads chikungunya, yellow fever and Zika (day-biting). Only the **female** mosquito bites for blood.

mistakes: Calling malaria a bacterial or viral disease — it is protozoan (Plasmodium).
Crediting Pasteur with the smallpox vaccine — that was Jenner; Pasteur made the rabies vaccine.
Thinking antibiotics cure viral infections — they act only on bacteria.
subtopics.notes:
### Disease → pathogen type
| Type | Diseases |
|---|---|
| **Bacteria** | **TB, cholera, typhoid, tetanus, leprosy, plague, whooping cough, anthrax** |
| **Virus** | **Dengue, chikungunya, rabies, polio, measles, mumps, AIDS, COVID-19, smallpox, influenza, jaundice (hepatitis)** |
| **Protozoa** | **Malaria, kala-azar, amoebiasis (dysentery), sleeping sickness** |
| **Fungus** | **Ringworm, athlete's foot** |
Memory hook: cholera–typhoid–TB–tetanus–leprosy–plague travel together as the bacterial six; dengue–rabies–polio–measles–AIDS as the viral five.

### Vectors — who carries what
**Female Anopheles** → **malaria** (Plasmodium). **Aedes aegypti** → **dengue, chikungunya, zika**. **Culex** → **filariasis/elephantiasis** (Wuchereria bancrofti). **Sandfly** → **kala-azar** (Leishmania). **Tsetse fly** → **sleeping sickness** (Trypanosoma). **Rat flea** → **plague**. Only the female mosquito bites. AIDS is NOT spread by mosquitoes — only by blood, unsafe sex and shared needles.

### Vaccines, antibiotics and the discoverers
**Edward Jenner** — the first **vaccine** (smallpox, 1796; the word comes from 'vacca', cow). **Louis Pasteur** — germ theory, pasteurisation, **rabies vaccine**. **Robert Koch** — the **TB bacterium** (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), also anthrax and cholera. **Alexander Fleming** — **penicillin, 1928**, the first antibiotic (mould *Penicillium notatum*); florey and Chain made it a medicine. **Banting and Best (1921)** — **insulin** for diabetes. **Ronald Ross** proved malaria is carried by mosquitoes (worked in India; Nobel 1902).

### Key numbers and controls
- Smallpox: the first disease **eradicated** — WHO declared it in **1980**.
- **BCG** vaccine → TB; **MMR** → measles-mumps-rubella; polio drops → **Pulse Polio** campaign.
- Normal haemoglobin ≈ **12–16 g/dL**; low → **anaemia**; genetic blood disorders: **thalassaemia, sickle-cell anaemia**.
- **Epidemic** = outbreak in a region; **pandemic** = worldwide (COVID-19); **endemic** = always present locally.
- Diseases spread through contaminated **water and food** (cholera, typhoid, jaundice) — safe drinking water and vaccination are the cheapest shields; **Joseph Lister** introduced **antiseptic surgery** (carbolic acid).

### Quick revision
- Bacterial six: TB, cholera, typhoid, tetanus, leprosy, plague. Viral five: dengue, rabies, polio, measles, AIDS. Protozoa: malaria, kala-azar, amoebiasis, sleeping sickness.
- Anopheles–malaria, Aedes–dengue, Culex–elephantiasis, sandfly–kala-azar, tsetse–sleeping sickness, rat flea–plague.
- Jenner smallpox vaccine 1796; Pasteur rabies; Koch TB; Fleming penicillin 1928; Banting & Best insulin.
- Smallpox eradicated 1980; BCG–TB; AIDS never by mosquitoes.

patterns.name: Disease → pathogen type
patterns.howToSpot: 'Tuberculosis is caused by a…', 'which of these is a viral / protozoan disease', 'ringworm is caused by…', odd-one-out among disease types.
patterns.logic:
1. Bacterial set: TB, cholera, typhoid, tetanus, leprosy, plague, whooping cough, anthrax.
2. Viral set: dengue, chikungunya, rabies, polio, measles, mumps, AIDS, influenza, hepatitis, smallpox, COVID-19.
3. Protozoa: malaria, kala-azar, amoebiasis, sleeping sickness. Fungus: ringworm, athlete's foot.
4. Odd-one-out trick: dengue is VIRAL, malaria is PROTOZOAN — both mosquito-borne, different microbes.
Why: classify the disease first, then check the options against its set.

example.q: **Ringworm** is caused by a —
example.solution: **Fungus** (not a worm, despite the name). Athlete's foot is the other classic fungal infection.

patterns.name: Vector → disease
patterns.howToSpot: 'Dengue is spread by which mosquito', 'malaria is transmitted by…', 'which fly causes sleeping sickness', 'elephantiasis is carried by…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Mosquito map: female **Anopheles → malaria**; **Aedes → dengue, chikungunya, zika**; **Culex → filariasis (elephantiasis)**.
2. Other vectors: sandfly → kala-azar; tsetse fly → sleeping sickness; rat flea → plague.
3. Only female mosquitoes bite (they need blood for eggs). AIDS never travels by mosquito.
Why: each vector has exactly one disease family — pair them and eliminate.

example.q: **Elephantiasis** (filariasis) is transmitted by —
example.solution: **Culex mosquito**, carrying the worm *Wuchereria bancrofti*. Aedes gives dengue, Anopheles gives malaria.

patterns.name: Vaccines and eradication
patterns.howToSpot: 'BCG protects against…', 'first vaccine / who invented vaccination', 'which disease was eradicated', 'MMR stands for', Pulse Polio questions.
patterns.logic:
1. Vaccine map: BCG–TB, MMR–measles/mumps/rubella, polio drops–Pulse Polio, rabies vaccine–Pasteur.
2. History: **Jenner, smallpox, 1796** — the first vaccine ('vacca' = cow); smallpox the first **eradicated** disease (WHO, 1980).
3. 'Vaccine' word root and the eradication year are the two most-repeated facts.

example.q: The first disease to be **eradicated** worldwide (WHO, 1980) was —
example.solution: **Smallpox**. Jenner's 1796 cowpox vaccine against it started immunology — 'vaccine' from *vacca*, cow.

patterns.name: Scientist → medicine/discovery
patterns.howToSpot: 'Penicillin was discovered by…', 'who discovered the TB bacterium', 'pasteurisation / germ theory', 'insulin was discovered by', 'who proved mosquitoes spread malaria'.
patterns.logic:
1. Fleming — penicillin (1928, from *Penicillium* mould). Koch — TB, cholera, anthrax bacteria. Pasteur — germ theory, pasteurisation, rabies vaccine.
2. Banting and Best — insulin (1921). Ronald Ross — mosquito-malaria link (Nobel 1902, work done in India).
3. Don't mix Koch (bacteriologist) with Pasteur (the wider germ theorist).

example.q: **Penicillin**, the first antibiotic, was discovered by —
example.solution: **Alexander Fleming** in 1928, from the mould *Penicillium notatum*. Florey and Chain later turned it into a usable drug.

patterns.name: Epidemic vocabulary and lifestyle diseases
patterns.howToSpot: 'A disease spread worldwide is a…', 'diabetes is caused by deficiency of…', 'AIDS is caused by / spread by', 'epidemic vs endemic vs pandemic'.
patterns.logic:
1. Scale words: endemic–local and constant; epidemic–regional outbreak; pandemic–worldwide (COVID-19, 1918 flu).
2. Diabetes: insulin deficiency (pancreas) — sugar stays in the blood. AIDS: HIV destroys helper T-cells; spread by blood/sex/needles, NOT touch or mosquitoes.
3. Cancer = uncontrolled cell division; hypertension = persistent high BP.

example.q: **COVID-19** spread across the world in 2020. Such a worldwide outbreak is called a —
example.solution: **Pandemic** — an epidemic that crosses countries and continents. Endemic diseases stay local; epidemics stay regional.

patterns.name: Health numbers and blood disorders
patterns.howToSpot: 'Normal haemoglobin range', 'normal WBC count', 'lifespan of RBC', 'sickle-cell / thalassaemia is a … disorder', questions that need 120 × counts.
patterns.logic:
1. Normal values: haemoglobin 12–16 g/dL; RBC ≈ 5 million/mm³; WBC ≈ 6,000–8,000/mm³; platelets ≈ 1.5–4 lakh/mm³; RBC life 120 days.
2. Genetic blood disorders: thalassaemia and sickle-cell anaemia — inherited, not infectious.
3. Low haemoglobin = anaemia (iron); abnormal WBC rise = leukaemia.
Why: memorise the three normal ranges; disorders hang off them.

example.q: The average lifespan of a **red blood cell** is —
example.solution: **120 days**; the spleen recycles the worn-out cells (its nickname: graveyard of RBCs).

subtopics.title: Classification, plants, hormones and animal facts
subtopics.concept:
### Classification
- **Carolus Linnaeus** — **father of taxonomy**; **binomial nomenclature** (genus + species, e.g. *Homo sapiens*).
- **R.H. Whittaker (1969)** — **five-kingdom** classification: **Monera** (bacteria), **Protista**, **Fungi**, **Plantae**, **Animalia**.
- Viruses are not placed in these kingdoms; they are 'living' only inside a host cell.

### Scientific names (frequently asked)
| Organism | Scientific name |
|---|---|
| Human | *Homo sapiens* |
| Mango | *Mangifera indica* |
| Tiger / Lion | *Panthera tigris* / *Panthera leo* |
| Peacock | *Pavo cristatus* |
| Neem | *Azadirachta indica* |
| Rice / Wheat | *Oryza sativa* / *Triticum aestivum* |
| Potato | *Solanum tuberosum* |
| Pea | *Pisum sativum* |
| Onion | *Allium cepa* |
| Banyan | *Ficus benghalensis* |
| Housefly | *Musca domestica* |

### Plant physiology
- **Photosynthesis** occurs in **chloroplasts** using **chlorophyll**; the **oxygen released comes from water**.
- **Xylem** carries **water and minerals** upward; **phloem** carries **food** (translocation).
- **Transpiration** — loss of water through **stomata**.
- **Nitrogen fixation** — **Rhizobium** bacteria in the **root nodules of legumes** (pulses); blue-green algae (e.g. *Anabaena*) in paddy fields.
- **Insectivorous plants**: **pitcher plant** (*Nepenthes*), Venus flytrap, sundew — they grow in nitrogen-poor soil. **Parasite**: *Cuscuta* (amarbel).

### Plant hormones
| Hormone | Main role |
|---|---|
| **Auxin** | Cell elongation, apical dominance, phototropism, rooting |
| **Gibberellin** | Stem elongation, seed germination, fruit size |
| **Cytokinin** | **Cell division**, delays ageing of leaves |
| **Abscisic acid (ABA)** | **'Stress hormone'** — dormancy, **closes stomata**, leaf fall |
| **Ethylene** | **Fruit ripening** (the only **gaseous** hormone) |

### Edible parts
| Plant | Edible part |
|---|---|
| **Potato** | **Stem** (tuber) |
| **Ginger, turmeric** | **Stem** (rhizome) |
| Onion | Bulb (fleshy leaf bases on a short stem) |
| **Carrot, radish, sweet potato, beetroot** | **Root** |
| **Cauliflower** | **Inflorescence** (flower) |
| **Apple** | **Thalamus** (false fruit) |
| **Mango** | Mesocarp |
| **Coconut** | **Endosperm** |
| Spinach, cabbage | Leaves |

### Animal facts
- Largest animal: **blue whale**. Largest bird: **ostrich**. Egg-laying mammals: **platypus, echidna**. The only mammal that truly flies: **bat**.
- Whales, dolphins and bats are **mammals**; fish breathe with **gills**; frogs are **amphibians**.
- **Cold-blooded**: fish, amphibians, reptiles. **Warm-blooded**: birds, mammals.
- Insects have **6 legs**; spiders have **8** (arachnids, not insects). The **earthworm** is the 'farmer's friend'.

tricks.title: Underground but not a root
tricks.body: **Potato, ginger, turmeric, onion** grow underground but are **stems** (they have nodes/buds or 'eyes'). **Carrot, radish, sweet potato, beetroot** are true **roots**.

example.q: The edible part of ginger is?
example.solution: A modified stem (rhizome).

tricks.title: Five kingdoms: 'My Pet Fish Plays Alone'

mistakes: Calling sweet potato a stem and potato a root — it is the other way round.
Saying the oxygen from photosynthesis comes from CO₂ — it comes from water.
Calling the bat a bird or the whale a fish — both are mammals.
subtopics.notes:
### Classification — the ladder
**Carolus Linnaeus**, the **father of taxonomy**, gave **binomial nomenclature** (two-word scientific name: genus + species, in italics — *Mangifera indica*). **R.H. Whittaker (1969)** gave the **five-kingdom** classification: **Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia** (earlier: two kingdoms, plants and animals). Plants divide into **cryptogams** (seedless — algae, fungi, bryophytes, pteridophytes) and **phanerogams** (seed plants — gymnosperms, naked seed; angiosperms, seed inside fruit). **Monocots** (wheat, rice, maize): one seed leaf, **parallel** leaf veins, fibrous roots. **Dicots** (mango, pea, gram): two seed leaves, **reticulate** veins, taproot.

### Plant hormones
**Auxin** — cell elongation, bending to light (**phototropism**). **Gibberellin** — stem elongation, seed germination. **Cytokinin** — cell division, delays leaf ageing. **Ethylene (gas)** — **fruit ripening**. **Abscisic acid** — the stress hormone: closes stomata, promotes wilting and dormancy.

### Photosynthesis and transport
Photosynthesis in the **chloroplast** (green pigment **chlorophyll**): **6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂** in sunlight. Leaves exchange gases through **stomata**; **transpiration** pulls water up the xylem (phloem carries food). Excess water vapour escapes mainly through the leaf's lower surface.

### Edible parts — the exam favourite
| Plant | Edible part |
|---|---|
| Carrot, radish, beetroot, turnip | **Root** |
| Potato, ginger, turmeric, onion (bulb), sugarcane | **Stem (modified)** |
| Cabbage, spinach, lettuce | **Leaves** |
| Cauliflower, broccoli | **Flower** |
| Tomato, brinjal, pumpkin, cucumber | **Fruit** |
| Groundnut, gram, mustard, rice, wheat | **Seed** |
| Apple, cashew | Fleshy **thalamus** (accessory fruit) |

### Reproduction and scientific names
Vegetative propagation: runners, bulbs, and human-made **grafting, layering, cutting, tissue culture**. Pollination agents: wind (maize, wheat — light dry pollen), water, insects (bright petals, nectar). Common scientific names: mango **Mangifera indica**, neem **Azadirachta indica**, banyan **Ficus benghalensis**, tamarind **Tamarindus indica**, potato **Solanum tuberosum**, rice **Oryza sativa**, tiger **Panthera tigris**, frog **Rana tigrina**.

### Quick revision
- Linnaeus = binomial nomenclature, father of taxonomy; Whittaker = 5 kingdoms (1969).
- Monocot: one cotyledon, parallel veins; dicot: two, reticulate veins.
- Auxin–elongation/phototropism; gibberellin–stem; cytokinin–division; ethylene–ripening; ABA–stress.
- Carrot root, potato/ginger/onion stem, cabbage leaf, cauliflower flower, tomato fruit, groundnut seed.
- Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → glucose + 6O₂; stomata = gas exchange; xylem water, phloem food.

patterns.name: Classification history and systems
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who gave binomial nomenclature / five-kingdom classification', 'which kingdom does a bacterium belong to', two-kingdom vs five-kingdom, cryptogam vs phanerogam.
patterns.logic:
1. **Linnaeus** — binomial nomenclature, father of taxonomy (species plantarum, 1753). **Whittaker (1969)** — five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
2. Bacteria sit in **Monera** (prokaryotes); moulds and mushrooms in Fungi.
3. Cryptogams = seedless (algae to ferns); phanerogams = seed-bearing (gymnosperms naked seed, angiosperms covered).
Why: one scientist = one system; the kingdom of bacteria is the standard trap.

example.q: The **five-kingdom** classification was proposed by —
example.solution: **R.H. Whittaker (1969)** — Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia. Linnaeus earlier gave binomial nomenclature.

patterns.name: Edible part of the plant
patterns.howToSpot: 'Potato is a modified…', 'carrot is which plant part', 'onion is a modified…', match-the-column of plants and their edible parts.
patterns.logic:
1. Roots: carrot, radish, beetroot, turnip, sweet potato.
2. Stems: potato (tuber), ginger/turmeric (rhizome), onion/garlic (bulb), sugarcane.
3. Leaves: cabbage, spinach, lettuce. Flower: cauliflower, broccoli. Fruit: tomato, brinjal, pumpkin. Seed: groundnut, gram, mustard.
4. The double trap: sweet potato is a ROOT, ordinary potato a STEM; onion is a bulb (stem with fleshy leaves).
Why: recall by family groups — roots cluster, stems cluster, one fruit list.

example.q: The **potato** we eat is a modified —
example.solution: **Stem** — an underground tuber with 'eyes' (buds). Sweet potato, despite the name, is a modified root.

patterns.name: Plant hormones
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which hormone ripens fruits', 'which hormone causes bending towards light', 'stress hormone of plants', 'which hormone promotes cell division'.
patterns.logic:
1. Auxin — elongation, phototropism (bending to light). Gibberellin — stem length, germination. Cytokinin — cell division, delays ageing.
2. **Ethylene (a gas) — fruit ripening**; abscisic acid — stress, stomatal closure, wilting.
3. Ripening = ethylene; bending = auxin; wilting = ABA — three fixed one-word answers.

example.q: The plant hormone responsible for **fruit ripening** is —
example.solution: **Ethylene** — the only gaseous plant hormone. Ripening bananas release it, so they can ripen other fruit kept nearby.

patterns.name: Photosynthesis and transport
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which gas is released in photosynthesis', 'which pigment absorbs light', 'xylem carries…', 'stomata are found on…', photosynthesis word equation.
patterns.logic:
1. 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ — inputs CO₂ + water, outputs glucose + **oxygen**; pigment = **chlorophyll** in chloroplasts.
2. **Xylem** carries water/minerals up; **phloem** carries food both ways.
3. **Stomata** (mostly on the leaf's lower surface) do gas exchange and transpiration.

example.q: In photosynthesis, plants **release** —
example.solution: **Oxygen**, splitting water in the chloroplast: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → glucose + 6O₂ in sunlight.

patterns.name: Monocot vs dicot and reproduction
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is a monocot', 'parallel venation indicates…', 'pollination by insects / wind', 'grafting is a method of…', number of cotyledons.
patterns.logic:
1. Monocots — wheat, rice, maize, onion: one cotyledon, parallel veins, fibrous roots. Dicots — mango, pea, gram, sunflower: two cotyledons, reticulate veins, taproot.
2. Insect pollination: bright petals + nectar + scent (mustard, rose). Wind: light dry pollen (maize, wheat).
3. Grafting, layering, cutting, tissue culture = vegetative (asexual) propagation.

example.q: Which of these shows **parallel venation** (a monocot)?
example.solution: **Maize/wheat/rice/onion** — monocots have parallel veins and fibrous roots; mango and pea are dicots with net-like veins.

patterns.name: Scientific names and firsts
patterns.howToSpot: 'The scientific name of mango / neem / rice', match-the-column of plants and binomials, father-of-taxonomy questions.
patterns.logic:
1. Mango *Mangifera indica*; neem *Azadirachta indica*; banyan *Ficus benghalensis*; tamarind *Tamarindus indica*.
2. Potato *Solanum tuberosum*; rice *Oryza sativa*; wheat *Triticum aestivum*; cat *Felis catus*; tiger *Panthera tigris*.
3. First word = genus (capital), second = species (small), both italic — the binomial rule of Linnaeus.

example.q: The scientific name of **mango** is —
example.solution: ***Mangifera indica*** — genus *Mangifera*, species *indica*. Neem is *Azadirachta indica*.
