### Culture / rearing
| Term | Rearing of |
|---|---|
| **Apiculture** | **Honey bees** |
| **Sericulture** | **Silkworms** (silk) |
| **Pisciculture** | **Fish** |
| **Viticulture** | **Grapes** |
| **Lac culture** | Lac insects |

### Ecology
- 'Ecology' was coined by **Ernst Haeckel**; 'ecosystem' by **A.G. Tansley (1935)**.
- A **food chain** runs: **producers** (green plants) → **primary consumers** (herbivores) → secondary consumers → tertiary consumers. **Decomposers** (bacteria, fungi) recycle nutrients.
- **10% law (Lindeman)**: only about **10% of energy** passes to the next trophic level; the rest is lost mostly as heat. Hence food chains are short (usually 3–5 levels).
- The **pyramid of energy is always upright**; the pyramid of biomass in a pond can be inverted.
- **Biomagnification** — non-degradable chemicals like **DDT** and mercury **increase in concentration** at higher trophic levels.
- The flow of energy is **one-way**; nutrients **cycle**.

formulas.name: 10% law of energy transfer
formulas.note: E₁ = energy at the producer level, n = trophic level

tricks.title: Culture words by root
tricks.body: **Api** = bee (apiary), **Seri** = silk, **Pisci** = fish (Pisces), **Viti** = vine/grapes, **Pomo** = fruit (pomegranate), **Olera** = vegetables.

example.q: Sericulture is the rearing of?
example.solution: Silkworms.

tricks.title: Study-of roots
tricks.body: **Ornitho** = bird, **Ento** = insect, **Ichthyo** = fish, **Herpeto** = creeping animals, **Myco** = fungus, **Phyco** = seaweed/algae, **Onco** = tumour, **Nephro** = kidney.

mistakes: Saying energy cycles in an ecosystem — it flows one way; nutrients cycle.
subtopics.notes:
### Branches of study — the -ology table
| Branch | Studies |
|---|---|
| **Ornithology** | **Birds** |
| **Entomology** | **Insects** |
| **Ichthyology** | **Fishes** |
| **Herpetology** | **Reptiles and amphibians** |
| **Mycology** | **Fungi** |
| **Virology** | Viruses |
| **Cytology** | Cells |
| **Histology** | Tissues |
| **Oncology** | Cancer |
| **Cardiology** | Heart |
| **Ophthalmology** | Eye |
| **Anthology** | Flowers |
Trap pair: en**tom**ology = insects (not etymology — words). Apiology = bees; malacology = molluscs.

### Culture words — rearing living things
**Apiculture** = honeybees (honey). **Sericulture** = silkworms (silk). **Pisciculture** = fish. **Aquaculture** = water organisms. **Horticulture** = garden plants. **Floriculture** = flowers. **Vermiculture** = earthworms. **Silviculture** = forest trees. **Poultry** farming = fowl. India's colour revolutions: **Green** — food grain (M.S. Swaminathan in India; Norman Borlaug worldwide), **White** — milk (**Verghese Kurien**, Operation Flood), **Blue** — fish, **Yellow** — oilseeds.

### Ecosystem and the 10% law
An **ecosystem** = living community + its physical surroundings. Food chain: **producers** (green plants) → **herbivores** (primary consumers) → **carnivores** (secondary, tertiary). **Lindeman's 10% law**: only about **10% of energy passes to the next level** — 10,000 J of producers gives 1,000 J to herbivores, 100 J to small carnivores, 10 J to big ones. **Decomposers** (bacteria, fungi) recycle nutrients. A **food web** is interlinked chains; **bioaccumulation** makes toxins concentrate up the chain.

### Cycles, conservation, biodiversity
**Nitrogen cycle**: soil nitrogen → plants (via **Rhizobium** bacteria in legume root nodules) → animals → back to soil. **Carbon cycle** ties respiration, photosynthesis and fuels. Conservation firsts: **Jim Corbett National Park (1936)** — India's first; **Project Tiger (1973)**; **Chipko movement (1973)** — villagers hugging trees. **IUCN Red List** ranks threatened species (extinct → vulnerable → least concern); the **Red Data Book** records them. Ramsar sites = wetlands.

### Pollution and milestones
Air: CO, SO₂, NOₓ, particulates; **BOD** (biochemical oxygen demand) measures water pollution — higher BOD, dirtier water. **Silent Spring** (Rachel Carson, 1962) warned against pesticides like **DDT**. Cloning milestone: **Dolly the sheep (1996)**, first cloned mammal. **Norman Borlaug** = father of the Green Revolution; **Salim Ali** = the birdman of India.

### Quick revision
- Ornithology–birds, entomology–insects, ichthyology–fish, herpetology–reptiles, mycology–fungi, oncology–cancer.
- Apiculture–bees, sericulture–silk, pisciculture–fish, vermiculture–worms, silviculture–trees.
- 10% law (Lindeman): 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 J up the chain.
- Corbett 1936 first park; Project Tiger 1973; Chipko 1973; Dolly the sheep 1996.
- Green–Swaminathan/Borlaug, White–Kurien, Blue–fish; Rhizobium fixes nitrogen in legume nodules.

patterns.name: Branch of study → organism
patterns.howToSpot: 'Ornithology is the study of…', 'entomology / ichthyology / herpetology / mycology', 'study of cancer / heart / eye', odd-one-out among -ology branches.
patterns.logic:
1. Animals: ornithology–birds, entomology–insects, ichthyology–fishes, herpetology–reptiles+amphibians, apiology–bees.
2. Micro/inner: mycology–fungi, virology–viruses, cytology–cells, histology–tissues.
3. Medical: oncology–cancer, cardiology–heart, ophthalmology–eye, nephrology–kidney.
4. Kill the trap: entomology is insects, NOT etymology (words).
Why: root + animal = answer; cluster-learn five at a time.

example.q: **Entomology** is the study of —
example.solution: **Insects**. Don't confuse with etymology (word origins). Ichthyology is fish; ornithology, birds.

patterns.name: Culture/rearing word ↔ creature
patterns.howToSpot: 'Sericulture is associated with…', 'apiculture / pisciculture / vermiculture', 'which culture is for flowers', match-the-column of cultures.
patterns.logic:
1. Apiculture–bees (honey); sericulture–silkworms (silk); pisciculture–fish; aquaculture–water organisms.
2. Horticulture–gardens; floriculture–flowers; vermiculture–earthworms; silviculture–trees.
3. Root logic helps: api- (bee), seri- (silk), pisci- (fish), vermi- (worm), silvi- (forest).
Why: each word is Latin root + culture; decode the root when unsure.

example.q: **Sericulture** is the rearing of —
example.solution: **Silkworms** for silk production. Apiculture keeps bees, pisciculture fish.

patterns.name: Food chain and the 10% law (computed)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Producers trap 10,000 J, energy at the third level', 'the 10% law was given by…', 'which are primary consumers', 'energy flow is always…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Chain: producers → primary (herbivores) → secondary → tertiary; energy flows one way, decreasing.
2. **Lindeman's 10% law**: keep chopping a zero — 10,000 J → 1,000 J (2nd level) → 100 J (3rd) → 10 J (4th) → 1 J (5th).
3. 'Third trophic level' = second consumer = small carnivores: 100 J from a 10,000 J base. Count levels, not names.

example.q: Producers store **10,000 J**. By the 10% law, the energy reaching the **third trophic level** is —
example.solution: 10,000 → 1,000 (herbivores) → **100 J** (small carnivores). Each step keeps only a tenth.

patterns.name: Conservation firsts and biodiversity
patterns.howToSpot: 'First national park of India', 'Project Tiger was launched in…', 'Chipko movement', 'IUCN Red List', 'which bacteria fix nitrogen in legumes'.
patterns.logic:
1. Jim Corbett (1936) = first national park; Project Tiger (1973); Chipko movement (1973, tree-hugging, Sunderlal Bahuguna).
2. IUCN Red List + Red Data Book = threatened species records; Ramsar = wetlands.
3. **Rhizobium** in legume root nodules fixes atmospheric nitrogen — the natural fertiliser.

example.q: India's **first national park** (1936) is —
example.solution: **Jim Corbett National Park** (Uttarakhand; originally Hailey). Project Tiger began there in 1973.

patterns.name: Colour revolutions and scientists
patterns.howToSpot: 'White Revolution is related to…', 'father of the Green Revolution', 'who is the birdman of India', 'Blue Revolution'.
patterns.logic:
1. Green–food grain (M.S. Swaminathan in India; Norman Borlaug worldwide); White–milk (Verghese Kurien, Operation Flood); Blue–fish; Yellow–oilseeds.
2. Salim Ali = birdman of India; Rachel Carson = *Silent Spring* (DDT warning); Dolly the sheep (1996) = first cloned mammal.
3. Pair the colour with the produce first, then attach the name.

example.q: The **White Revolution** (Operation Flood) in India is associated with —
example.solution: **Milk production**, led by **Verghese Kurien** (Amul). Green was food grain, Blue was fish.

patterns.name: Ecology basics and pollution measures
patterns.howToSpot: 'BOD measures…', 'which organisms are decomposers', 'ozone layer position', 'food web is…', 'bioaccumulation'.
patterns.logic:
1. **BOD** (biochemical oxygen demand) — higher value = more polluted water.
2. Decomposers = bacteria and fungi recycling nutrients; food web = many interlinked food chains.
3. Pollutants like DDT **bioaccumulate** up the food chain — top predators get the most.
4. Ozone layer sits in the stratosphere; CFCs were its destroyer (Montreal Protocol, 1987).

example.q: **BOD** (biochemical oxygen demand) of a water sample indicates —
example.solution: Its **pollution level**: more organic waste means bacteria consume more oxygen, so a HIGHER BOD means dirtier water.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Scurvy / rickets / goitre / anaemia is caused by deficiency of…', 'which vitamin is fat-soluble', kwashiorkor vs marasmus, wrong-pair questions on the vitamin table.
pyqPatterns.approach: Sing the ladder: A–night blindness, B₁–beriberi, B₃–pellagra, B₁₂–pernicious anaemia, C–scurvy, D–rickets, E–sterility, K–clotting. Fat-soluble = A, D, E, K. Minerals: iron–anaemia, iodine–goitre, calcium–bones. Kwashiorkor = protein lack (swollen), marasmus = protein + calories (shrunken).

example.q: Deficiency of vitamin C causes:
example.solution: Scurvy — bleeding gums and slow healing. Sailors avoided it with citrus; amla is the richest Indian source.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Dengue / malaria / TB is caused by or spread by…', 'which of these is a viral disease', 'elephantiasis is transmitted by', odd-one-out among pathogens.
pyqPatterns.approach: Classify first: bacteria (TB, cholera, typhoid, tetanus, leprosy, plague), virus (dengue, rabies, polio, measles, AIDS), protozoa (malaria, kala-azar, amoebiasis), fungus (ringworm). Vectors: Anopheles–malaria, Aedes–dengue/chikungunya, Culex–elephantiasis, sandfly–kala-azar, tsetse–sleeping sickness, rat flea–plague. Dengue (viral) and malaria (protozoan) both ride mosquitoes but are different microbes — the favourite odd-one-out.

example.q: Which mosquito transmits dengue?
example.solution: Aedes aegypti — it bites by day and also carries chikungunya and zika. Malaria rides the female Anopheles instead.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Largest gland / largest organ / longest bone / smallest bone', 'universal blood donor', 'bile is produced in', 'pace-maker of the heart', 'how many bones in an adult'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Records: skin largest organ, liver largest gland, thyroid largest endocrine gland, femur longest bone, stapes smallest bone, 206 adult bones. Blood: O− universal donor, AB+ universal recipient, platelets clot, SA node pace-maker. Secretions: liver makes bile (gall bladder stores it, no enzymes), stomach HCl + pepsin, pancreas insulin + trypsin. Pituitary is the master gland; thyroxine needs iodine.

example.q: The smallest bone in the human body is:
example.solution: Stapes, in the middle ear. The largest gland is the liver and the longest bone the femur — keep the three records separate.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Who discovered penicillin / the cell / the vaccine', 'insulin was discovered by', 'who proved mosquitoes carry malaria', match-the-column of biologists.
pyqPatterns.approach: Timeline table: Hooke–cell (1665), Leeuwenhoek–living cells, Brown–nucleus, Schleiden + Schwann–cell theory, Virchow–omnis cellula; Jenner–first vaccine (smallpox, 1796), Pasteur–rabies vaccine and pasteurisation, Koch–TB bacterium, Fleming–penicillin (1928), Banting & Best–insulin (1921), Ross–mosquito-malaria link, Mendel–genetics, Watson & Crick–DNA double helix.

example.q: Who discovered penicillin?
example.solution: Alexander Fleming, in 1928, from the mould Penicillium notatum. Koch identified the TB bacterium; Pasteur gave the rabies vaccine.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Powerhouse of the cell / suicide bags', 'which organelle makes protein', 'human body cell has how many chromosomes', 'sex of the child is determined by', 'Mendel worked on'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Nickname pairs: mitochondria–powerhouse, ribosome–protein factory, lysosome–suicide bag, Golgi–post office; mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA. Genetics: 46 chromosomes (23 pairs), meiosis halves to 23 in gametes, XX female / XY male so the father decides sex; Mendel = father of genetics (pea plant), Watson & Crick = DNA double helix.

example.q: The sex of a child is determined by:
example.solution: The father's sperm — it carries either X (girl, XX) or Y (boy, XY); the mother's egg always gives X.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Ornithology / entomology / sericulture / apiculture is the study or rearing of', 'study of cancer', 'ichthyology', match-the-column of -ology words.
pyqPatterns.approach: Branches: ornithology–birds, entomology–insects (not etymology!), ichthyology–fish, herpetology–reptiles and amphibians, mycology–fungi, cytology–cells, oncology–cancer, cardiology–heart. Cultures: apiculture–bees, sericulture–silkworms, pisciculture–fish, vermiculture–earthworms, horticulture–gardens. Decode the Latin root when unsure (api-, seri-, pisci-).

example.q: Sericulture is associated with:
example.solution: Rearing silkworms for silk. Apiculture keeps bees, pisciculture farms fish — root + culture decodes each word.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Plant hormones, edible parts and classification
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which hormone ripens fruit / bends shoots to light', 'potato / carrot / onion is a modified…', 'five-kingdom classification', 'monocot vs dicot', 'xylem carries…'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Hormones: auxin–elongation and phototropism, gibberellin–stem growth, cytokinin–cell division, ethylene–fruit ripening, abscisic acid–stress. Edible parts: carrot–root, potato/ginger/onion–stem, cabbage–leaf, cauliflower–flower, tomato–fruit, groundnut–seed. Classification: Linnaeus–binomial, Whittaker–5 kingdoms, bacteria in Monera; monocot one cotyledon + parallel veins, dicot two + reticulate; xylem water up, phloem food.

example.q: Which plant hormone is a gas that ripens fruit?
example.solution: Ethylene — a ripe banana releases it and ripens neighbouring fruit. Auxin bends shoots toward light; ABA closes stomata under stress.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'The scientific name of mango / neem / rice / tiger', 'in binomial nomenclature the first word is', italics and capitalisation rules.
pyqPatterns.approach: Binomial = Genus (capital) + species (small), both italics. Mango Mangifera indica, neem Azadirachta indica, banyan Ficus benghalensis, tamarind Tamarindus indica, potato Solanum tuberosum, rice Oryza sativa, tiger Panthera tigris, frog Rana tigrina. Watch the two *-indica* pairings: mango and neem share the species name, not the genus.

example.q: In Mangifera indica, the word Mangifera denotes the:
example.solution: Genus — the first, capitalised word; indica is the species. The binomial system is Linnaeus's.

solvedExamples.solution: Vitamin C (**ascorbic acid**) is needed to make collagen; its deficiency causes **scurvy** — bleeding and swollen gums, slow wound healing. Rickets is vitamin D, beriberi is B1 and night blindness is A.

solvedExamples.q: Which blood group is known as the universal donor?
solvedExamples.solution: Group **O** red cells carry **no A or B antigens**, so they are not attacked by the recipient's anti-A or anti-B antibodies — **O is the universal donor** (strictly O negative). **AB** is the universal recipient.
Malaria is caused by the **protozoan *Plasmodium*** and spread by the bite of an infected **female Anopheles** mosquito. Ronald Ross proved the mosquito link (Nobel 1902).

solvedExamples.q: The edible part of the potato is a:
solvedExamples.solution: The potato is a **tuber — a modified underground stem**. Its 'eyes' are buds at nodes, which roots do not have. Sweet potato, by contrast, is a modified root.

practice.q: Which organelle is known as the 'powerhouse of the cell'?
practice.solution: **Mitochondria** carry out aerobic respiration and produce **ATP**, the cell's energy currency — hence 'powerhouse'. Ribosomes make proteins and lysosomes are the 'suicide bags'.

practice.q: Who first discovered the cell, in 1665?
practice.solution: **Robert Hooke** observed box-like compartments in a thin slice of **cork** in 1665 and called them 'cells'. Robert Brown discovered the nucleus (1831) and Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells.

practice.q: In a food chain, producers trap 10,000 J of energy. According to the 10% law, how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
practice.solution: Only about **10%** passes to each next level: producers 10,000 J → primary consumers 1,000 J → **secondary consumers 100 J**.

practice.q: Which is the largest gland in the human body?
practice.solution: The **liver** is the largest gland (and largest internal organ). It secretes bile, stores glycogen and detoxifies substances. The pituitary is the 'master gland', not the largest.

practice.q: The smallest bone in the human body is:
practice.solution: The **stapes** (stirrup) in the **middle ear** is the smallest bone. The femur (thigh bone) is the longest. Malleus and incus are the other two ear ossicles, both larger than the stapes.

practice.q: Insulin is secreted by:
practice.solution: **Insulin** is secreted by the **β-cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas**. It lowers blood glucose; lack of it causes **diabetes mellitus**.

practice.q: Rickets in children is caused by deficiency of:
practice.solution: **Vitamin D (calciferol)** helps absorb calcium and phosphorus. Without it bones stay soft and bend — **rickets** in children, osteomalacia in adults. Sunlight lets the skin make vitamin D.

practice.q: Goitre is caused by deficiency of:
practice.solution: **Iodine** is needed to make **thyroxine**. When it is short, the thyroid gland enlarges — **goitre**. Iron deficiency causes anaemia.

practice.q: Vitamin K is essential for:
practice.solution: **Vitamin K** is needed to make clotting factors (such as prothrombin) in the liver; its deficiency leads to excessive bleeding. Vision needs vitamin A, gums need C, bones need D.

practice.q: Dengue fever is transmitted by which mosquito?
practice.solution: **Dengue** (a viral disease) is spread by the day-biting **Aedes** mosquito (*Aedes aegypti*), which also spreads chikungunya, Zika and yellow fever. Anopheles spreads malaria and Culex spreads filariasis.

practice.q: Penicillin, the first antibiotic, was discovered by:
practice.solution: **Alexander Fleming** discovered penicillin in **1928** from the mould *Penicillium notatum*. Jenner made the smallpox vaccine, Pasteur the rabies vaccine, and Koch discovered the TB bacterium.

practice.q: Tuberculosis is caused by a:
practice.solution: TB is caused by the bacterium ***Mycobacterium tuberculosis***, discovered by Robert Koch (1882). The **BCG** vaccine protects against it and the **Mantoux** test detects infection.

practice.q: Which plant hormone is responsible for the ripening of fruits?
practice.solution: **Ethylene**, a gaseous hormone, speeds up **fruit ripening**. Auxin controls cell elongation, cytokinin promotes cell division and gibberellin causes stem elongation.

practice.q: The five-kingdom classification of living organisms was proposed by:
practice.solution: **R.H. Whittaker** proposed the five kingdoms — Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — in **1969**. Linnaeus gave binomial nomenclature and the two-kingdom system.
practice.shortcut: My Pet Fish Plays Alone — Whittaker.

practice.q: Ornithology is the study of:
practice.solution: **Ornithology** is the study of **birds** (Greek *ornis*, bird). Insects — entomology, fish — ichthyology, fungi — mycology.

practice.q: Who first saw and named **'cells'** in cork (1665)?
practice.solution: **Robert Hooke**, in *Micrographia* (1665), saw box-like dead cork walls and named them cells. Leeuwenhoek later saw living cells.

practice.q: The **nucleus** was discovered by —
practice.solution: **Robert Brown (1831)** found the nucleus inside orchid cells. Schleiden and Schwann built the cell theory; Virchow added 'cells from cells'.

practice.q: *Omnis cellula e cellula* (every cell from a pre-existing cell) was stated by —
practice.solution: **Virchow (1855)** completed the cell theory with this line. Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) had proposed the theory itself.

practice.q: The **'powerhouse of the cell'** is —
practice.solution: **Mitochondria** run respiration and make ATP — hence the powerhouse. They also carry their own DNA.

practice.q: **Protein synthesis** in a cell is done by —
practice.solution: **Ribosomes** are the 'protein factories'. Lysosomes digest; chloroplasts photosynthesise.

practice.q: Which organelles contain their **own DNA**, apart from the nucleus?
practice.solution: **Mitochondria and chloroplasts** are semi-autonomous — both keep their own circular DNA, a sign of their bacterial ancestors.

practice.q: Which structure is **absent in animal cells**?
practice.solution: A **cellulose cell wall** is plant-only (with chloroplasts and a big central vacuole). Animal cells have a centrosome instead.

practice.q: Which of these is a **prokaryote**?
practice.solution: **Bacteria** (and blue-green algae) have no true nucleus — prokaryotes. Amoeba, fungi and plants are eukaryotes.

practice.q: A normal **human body cell** contains how many chromosomes?
practice.solution: **46 chromosomes = 23 pairs**; 22 pairs are autosomes, the 23rd pair carries the sex chromosomes XX or XY.

practice.q: During **meiosis**, the chromosome number of a human cell —
practice.solution: **Meiosis** halves the number to make gametes (23); **mitosis** keeps 46 for growth. Fertilisation adds 23 + 23 back to 46.

practice.q: Who is called the **father of genetics**?
practice.solution: **Mendel**, an Austrian monk, deduced the laws of inheritance from garden-pea experiments. Darwin gave evolution; Watson and Crick, the DNA model.

practice.q: Mendel's experiments on heredity were performed on —
practice.solution: **Pisum sativum** — seven clear pairs of contrasting traits (tall/dwarf, round/wrinkled…). The fruit fly was Morgan's genetics workhorse later.

practice.q: The **sex of a child** is determined by —
practice.solution: The mother's egg always carries X; the father's sperm carries X (girl, XX) or Y (boy, XY) — so the **father determines sex**.

practice.q: The **double-helix model of DNA** was proposed by —
practice.solution: **James Watson and Francis Crick**, 1953. A gene is a segment of this DNA that codes one trait.

practice.q: The **largest cell** in the human body is —
practice.solution: The **ovum** is the largest; the **nerve cell** is the longest (up to about a metre). RBCs are among the smallest.

practice.q: Which blood cells **lack a nucleus** and carry oxygen?
practice.solution: Mature **RBCs** throw out their nucleus to pack in more **haemoglobin** (iron-based oxygen carrier). WBCs have nuclei and fight infection.

practice.q: The **largest gland** in the human body is —
practice.solution: **Liver** — largest gland and largest internal organ. The thyroid is only the largest ENDOCRINE gland.

practice.q: The **longest bone** in the human body is the —
practice.solution: **Femur** (thigh bone). The humerus is the upper arm; tibia and radius are lower leg and forearm bones.

practice.q: An adult human skeleton has how many bones?
practice.solution: **206** in an adult; a newborn starts near 300 and many fuse as it grows. Ribs add 12 pairs to the count.

practice.q: The **smallest muscle** in the human body is —
practice.solution: **Stapedius** in the middle ear moves the stapes bone. The masseter (jaw) is the strongest by force.

practice.q: The **universal donor** blood group is —
practice.solution: **O−** has no A, B or Rh antigens, so nobody's blood rejects it. AB+ is the universal recipient.

practice.q: Blood **clotting** is carried out by —
practice.solution: **Platelets (thrombocytes)** gather at a cut and trigger fibrin formation. WBC fight germs; RBC carry oxygen.

practice.q: The natural **pace-maker of the heart** is —
practice.solution: The **SA node** in the right atrium fires the beat — artificial pace-makers only replace it when it fails.

practice.q: Blood pressure is measured with a —
practice.solution: **Sphygmomanometer** — normal value 120/80 mm Hg (systolic/diastolic). A barometer measures air pressure.

practice.q: **Insulin**, which controls blood sugar, is secreted by the —
practice.solution: The **pancreas** (islets of Langerhans) secretes insulin; its shortage causes **diabetes**. The liver stores glycogen but makes no insulin.

practice.q: Bile is **stored** in the —
practice.solution: Made in the **liver**, stored in the **gall bladder**, released into the small intestine. Bile itself has no enzymes — it only emulsifies fat.

practice.q: The functional (filtering) unit of the **kidney** is the —
practice.solution: Each kidney packs about a million **nephrons**. Alveolus belongs to the lung, villus to the gut, neuron to nerves.

practice.q: Which part of the **brain** controls balance and posture?
practice.solution: **Cerebellum** — balance and coordinated movement. Cerebrum thinks; medulla runs heartbeat and breathing involuntarily.

practice.q: **Goitre**, a swelling of the neck, is caused by the deficiency of —
practice.solution: Iodised salt prevents it. The **thyroid** needs iodine to make **thyroxine**; without it the gland swells working harder.

practice.q: **Adrenaline**, the 'fight-or-flight' hormone, is secreted by the —
practice.solution: **Adrenal glands** (on the kidneys) release adrenaline in emergencies — faster heartbeat, more blood sugar, instant energy.

practice.q: Over-secretion of **growth hormone** in children causes —
practice.solution: Too much growth hormone from the pituitary in childhood → **gigantism**; too little → dwarfism; in adults, acromegaly.

practice.q: Which enzyme in **saliva** starts digesting starch?
practice.solution: **Salivary amylase** breaks starch while you chew. Pepsin and trypsin take protein; lipase takes fat.

practice.q: The enzyme **pepsin**, active in the stomach, digests —
practice.solution: **Pepsin** needs the stomach's **HCl** (strong acid) to work on protein. Amylase handles starch and lipase fat.

practice.q: A person's heart beats at **72 per minute**. Roughly how many beats is that in a **day**?
practice.solution: 72 × 60 = 4,320 per hour; × 24 = **103,680** per day — about 1 lakh beats daily.

practice.q: Normal human body temperature of **37 °C** equals —
practice.solution: F = 9 × 37/5 + 32 = 66.6 + 32 = **98.6 °F** — the standard body-temperature pair.

practice.q: **Rickets** in children is caused by the deficiency of —
practice.solution: **Vitamin D** (with calcium) hardens bones; its lack bends them — rickets. In adults the same lack gives osteomalacia.

practice.q: **Scurvy** (bleeding gums) is caused by the deficiency of —
practice.solution: **Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)** — sailors got scurvy on long voyages without fresh citrus. Amla is the richest Indian source.

practice.q: **Beriberi** results from the deficiency of —
practice.solution: **B₁ (thiamine)** — common where polished rice replaces whole grain. B₃ gives pellagra; B₂ cheilosis.

practice.q: **Night blindness** is an early sign of the deficiency of —
practice.solution: **Vitamin A (retinol)** — carrots and papaya are rich sources; advanced lack causes xerophthalmia and corneal damage.

practice.q: **Pellagra** is caused by the deficiency of —
practice.solution: **B₃ (niacin)** — the '3 Ds': dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia (and death if untreated). Groundnut is a good source.

practice.q: **Vitamin K** deficiency mainly causes —
practice.solution: **K = Koagulation** — the liver needs it to make clotting factors. Green leafy vegetables supply it.

practice.q: Which group is **entirely fat-soluble**?
practice.solution: **A, D, E, K** — they store in fat and liver, so excess can be toxic. B-complex and C are water-soluble and need daily intake.

practice.q: Which vitamin is synthesised in the **skin** on exposure to sunlight?
practice.solution: UV light converts a skin sterol into **vitamin D** — the 'sunshine vitamin'. Deficiency gives rickets (children) and osteomalacia (adults).

practice.q: The richest common Indian source of **vitamin C** is —
practice.solution: **Amla** tops the list (with guava close behind). Citrus fruits are famous but amla has several times more.

practice.q: **Goitre** is caused by the deficiency of —
practice.solution: **Iodine** is part of thyroxine; without it the thyroid swells. Iodised salt is the prevention.

practice.q: **Anaemia** is chiefly caused by the deficiency of —
practice.solution: **Iron** builds the haemoglobin that carries oxygen; low iron → pale, tired, breathless. Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency gives the rarer pernicious anaemia.

practice.q: **Fluorosis** (mottling of teeth and bones) is caused by —
practice.solution: **Too much fluorine** in drinking water causes fluorosis; a little protects against dental caries — the dose makes the poison.

practice.q: **Kwashiorkor** is caused by the severe deficiency of —
practice.solution: **Protein deficiency** with enough calories — swollen belly and oedema in children aged 1–3. Marasmus lacks protein AND calories.

practice.q: **Marasmus** differs from kwashiorkor because in marasmus the child lacks —
practice.solution: **Marasmus = protein + calorie deficiency** — the infant is wasted, skin and bones, under a year old. Kwashiorkor children swell instead.

practice.q: Which nutrient gives the **maximum energy per gram**?
practice.solution: **Fat — 9 kcal/g**, more than double carbohydrate or protein. That is why the body stores spare energy as fat.

practice.q: A food packet contains **30 g carbohydrate** and **10 g protein**. Its total energy is —
practice.solution: Carb 30 × 4 = 120 kcal; protein 10 × 4 = 40 kcal; total = **160 kcal**. Had it been fat, each gram would count 9.

practice.q: The word **'vitamine'** was coined by —
practice.solution: **Casimir Funk (1912)** coined 'vitamine' while studying beriberi. Fleming discovered penicillin — a different hall of fame.

practice.q: **Ascorbic acid** is the chemical name of —
practice.solution: **Vitamin C = ascorbic acid**. Retinol–A, calciferol–D, tocopherol–E, thiamine–B₁, cyanocobalamin–B₁₂.

practice.q: **Tuberculosis** is caused by a —
practice.solution: **Mycobacterium tuberculosis** — a bacterium, identified by Robert Koch. BCG vaccination protects against it.

practice.q: Which of these is a **protozoan** disease?
practice.solution: **Malaria** — the parasite *Plasmodium* is a protozoan. Dengue is viral, TB bacterial, ringworm fungal.

practice.q: **Cholera** and **typhoid** are caused by —
practice.solution: Both are **bacterial**, water/food-borne: *Vibrio cholerae* and *Salmonella typhi* — the classic unsafe-water pair.

practice.q: **Dengue** is transmitted by the —
practice.solution: **Aedes aegypti** carries dengue (and chikungunya, zika) — it bites by day. Anopheles gives malaria.

practice.q: **Malaria** is spread by the bite of —
practice.solution: The **female Anopheles** injects *Plasmodium*; Ronald Ross proved the link in India. Only female mosquitoes bite.

practice.q: **Sleeping sickness** is transmitted by the —
practice.solution: The **tsetse fly** (African) carries *Trypanosoma*. The sandfly gives kala-azar; the rat flea, plague.

practice.q: **Kala-azar** (visceral leishmaniasis) is spread by the —
practice.solution: The **sandfly** carries the protozoan *Leishmania*. Fever with spleen enlargement is the signature.

practice.q: The **BCG vaccine** protects against —
practice.solution: **BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin)** — given at birth against TB. Polio drops and MMR cover the other diseases.

practice.q: The **first vaccine** ever developed was against —
practice.solution: **Edward Jenner, 1796**, against smallpox — from 'vacca' (cow) comes the word vaccine. Smallpox was also the first eradicated disease.

practice.q: The **MMR vaccine** protects against —
practice.solution: **MMR = measles, mumps, rubella** (German measles) — a live-virus shot given in childhood.

practice.q: **Penicillin** was discovered by —
practice.solution: **Fleming, 1928** — noticed mould killing bacteria in a forgotten dish. Pasteur gave germ theory; Jenner, the first vaccine.

practice.q: The bacterium causing **tuberculosis** was discovered by —
practice.solution: **Robert Koch** — the TB bacillus (1882), plus anthrax and cholera bacteria. Pasteur is the wider germ-theory man.

practice.q: **Insulin** was discovered by —
practice.solution: **Frederick Banting and Charles Best (1921)** isolated insulin — turning diabetes from a death sentence into a manageable condition.

practice.q: A disease outbreak restricted to one **region** is an —
practice.solution: **Epidemic** = regional outbreak; **pandemic** = worldwide (COVID-19); **endemic** = permanently local (malaria in some districts).

practice.q: **AIDS** is NOT transmitted by —
practice.solution: HIV travels in blood and body fluids — never by mosquito bite, touch or shared meals. The virus destroys helper T-cells.

practice.q: The average lifespan of a human **red blood cell** is —
practice.solution: **120 days** — the spleen then recycles them, hence its nickname 'graveyard of RBCs'.

practice.q: **Sickle-cell anaemia** is a —
practice.solution: It is **inherited** — a gene fault makes RBCs sickle-shaped, so they clog capillaries. Thalassaemia is the other famous genetic blood disorder.

practice.q: The **five-kingdom** classification was proposed by —
practice.solution: **Whittaker (1969)**: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia. Linnaeus gave binomial nomenclature.

practice.q: Who is called the **father of taxonomy**?
practice.solution: **Linnaeus** — he introduced binomial nomenclature (*Species Plantarum*, 1753): a two-word scientific name for every organism.

practice.q: In the five-kingdom system, **bacteria** belong to the kingdom —
practice.solution: **Monera** holds the prokaryotes — bacteria and blue-green algae. Protista is single-celled eukaryotes like Amoeba.

practice.q: The **potato** is a modified —
practice.solution: An underground **stem tuber** — the 'eyes' are buds. Sweet potato is the root; the two are the classic pair.

practice.q: **Carrot** is an example of an edible —
practice.solution: **Taproot**, swollen with stored food — like radish, beetroot, turnip. Ginger is the stem-side answer.

practice.q: The **onion bulb** is mainly a modified —
practice.solution: A **bulb** — a compressed underground stem ringed by fleshy scale leaves. Garlic is its cousin.

practice.q: Which part of the plant do we eat in **cauliflower**?
practice.solution: Cauliflower (and broccoli) is a cluster of **undeveloped flower buds**. Cabbage is the leaf; the tomato a fruit.

practice.q: The plant hormone that **ripens fruit** is —
practice.solution: **Ethylene** — a gas; a ripe banana in a closed box ripens the raw fruit beside it. Auxin elongates; ABA stresses.

practice.q: Bending of a shoot **towards light** (phototropism) is caused by —
practice.solution: **Auxin** collects on the shaded side and elongates those cells, so the shoot bends toward light. ABA instead closes stomata under stress.

practice.q: Which hormone promotes **cell division** in plants?
practice.solution: **Cytokinin** — it drives cell division and delays leaf ageing (coconut water is rich in it). Gibberellin stretches stems.

practice.q: The gas **released during photosynthesis** is —
practice.solution: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ — the oxygen comes from splitting water. Respiration consumes oxygen instead.

practice.q: Which tissue carries **water** upward from the roots?
practice.solution: **Xylem** = water and minerals, upward; **phloem** = food, both directions. Stomata are pores, not transport tissue.

practice.q: The green pigment essential for photosynthesis is —
practice.solution: **Chlorophyll** in the chloroplasts traps sunlight; it is the reason leaves are green.

practice.q: Which of these is a **monocot** plant?
practice.solution: **Wheat** (and rice, maize, onion) — one seed leaf, parallel veins. Mango, pea and gram are dicots.

practice.q: **Grafting** is a method of —
practice.solution: A stem scion is joined to a rooted stock — no seeds, so the fruit keeps the parent's quality (mango, rose). Layering and cutting are its cousins.

practice.q: The scientific name of **neem** is —
practice.solution: ***Azadirachta indica***. Mango is *Mangifera indica*, banyan *Ficus benghalensis*, rice *Oryza sativa*.

practice.q: In binomial nomenclature, the **first word** of the scientific name denotes the —
practice.solution: Genus first (capitalised), species second (small), both in italics — e.g. *Mangifera indica*. The rule is Linnaeus's.

practice.q: **Ornithology** is the study of —
practice.solution: **Ornithology = birds** (Salim Ali, the birdman of India, was its greatest name here). Entomology is insects.

practice.q: **Ichthyology** is the study of —
practice.solution: **Ichthyology = fishes**. Mycology is fungi; cytology, cells; histology, tissues.

practice.q: **Mycology** is the study of —
practice.solution: **Mycology = fungi** — yeasts, moulds, mushrooms. Virology studies viruses.

practice.q: **Oncology** is the branch of medicine dealing with —
practice.solution: **Oncology = cancer** study and treatment. Cardiology–heart, nephrology–kidney, ophthalmology–eye.

practice.q: **Apiculture** is associated with the rearing of —
practice.solution: **Apiculture = bee-keeping** for honey and wax. Sericulture is silkworms; pisciculture, fish.

practice.q: **Sericulture** is related to —
practice.solution: **Sericulture** rears silkworms on mulberry leaves to produce raw silk.

practice.q: **Pisciculture** deals with —
practice.solution: **Pisciculture = fish culture** (the Blue Revolution). Vermiculture rears earthworms; silviculture, trees.

practice.q: Producers in a food chain trap **10,000 J** of energy. By the **10% law**, the energy at the **third trophic level** is —
practice.solution: 10% each step: 10,000 → **1,000 J** (primary consumers) → **100 J** (secondary carnivores = 3rd level) → 10 J (4th).

practice.q: The **10% law** of energy flow in ecosystems was given by —
practice.solution: **Raymond Lindeman** — only about a tenth of the energy passes to the next trophic level. Odum wrote the classic ecology textbook; Tansley coined 'ecosystem'.

practice.q: In a food chain, **green plants** are called —
practice.solution: **Producers** — they make food by photosynthesis and feed the whole chain; animals are consumers, bacteria and fungi the decomposers.

practice.q: India's **first national park**, set up in 1936, is —
practice.solution: **Jim Corbett** (Uttarakhand, first named Hailey) — 1936. Kaziranga holds rhinos, Gir the lions, Kanha tigers.

practice.q: **Project Tiger** was launched in —
practice.solution: **Project Tiger, 1973**, started from Corbett. The **Chipko movement** is also 1973 — tree-hugging villagers of Uttarakhand.

practice.q: Which bacterium fixes atmospheric **nitrogen in legume root nodules**?
practice.solution: **Rhizobium** lives in pea/gram/bean nodules and turns N₂ into usable compounds — why farmers rotate legumes.

practice.q: The **Green Revolution** in India is associated with —
practice.solution: **M.S. Swaminathan** led India's Green Revolution (high-yield wheat/rice); **Norman Borlaug** is its world father. Kurien = White Revolution (milk).

practice.q: The **White Revolution** (Operation Flood) made India self-sufficient in —
practice.solution: **Milk** — Operation Flood, led by **Verghese Kurien** (Amul). Blue = fish, Yellow = oilseeds, Green = food grain.

practice.q: Who is known as the **'birdman of India'**?
practice.solution: **Salim Ali** — the great ornithologist whose bird surveys and books mapped India's birdlife.

practice.q: **Dolly the sheep** (1996) is famous as the first —
practice.solution: **Dolly** — the first mammal cloned from an adult cell (Roslin Institute, Scotland, 1996), a landmark of biotechnology.

practice.q: A **higher BOD** value of a water sample means the water is —
practice.solution: **Biochemical oxygen demand** — more organic waste feeds more bacteria, which gulp more oxygen: high BOD = dirty water.
